cur:catacombs-nunziatella-christ-judge.summary: Wilpert's photograph shows the damaged vault of a small chamber painted with concentric circles and compartments; in the central field Christ sits as judge, with figures turned towards him in the surrounding fields. The chamber took its name from this vault painting, an early attempt to picture the judgment of the soul by Christ.
facts: Italian Wikipedia calls the main monument of this small rural catacomb the 'cubiculum of the Judgment', fully painted and dating to the second half of the 3rd century.
The catacomb was discovered by Giovanni Battista de Rossi in 1877; it contains no martyrs' tombs and served a small rural community.
Painting reproduced from Joseph Wilpert, Die Malereien der Katakomben Roms (Freiburg, 1903) (plate 75).
cur:catacombs-nunziatella-christ-judge.notes: Much of the vault is lost; the identification of the central figure as Christ the Judge follows Wilpert and later scholarship.

cur:manuscripts-paris-gregory-christ-ent.summary: The book opens with a full-page image of Christ seated frontally on a lyre-backed throne with a cushion, a great cross-nimbus behind his head; he blesses with his right hand and holds an open Gospel book on his knee. Much of the paint has flaked away, revealing the underdrawing of his robes, but the majestic, iconic figure remains clear. Placed before the imperial portraits, it presents Christ as the true ruler from whom earthly authority descends.
facts: The frontispiece Christ is followed by portraits of the Empress Eudokia with her sons and of Emperor Basil I, so that the imperial family appears under Christ's authority.

The Paris Gregory was commissioned by Patriarch Photios as a gift for Emperor Basil I between 879 and 883 and is one of the most ambitious Byzantine manuscripts to survive from the generation after Iconoclasm.
cur:manuscripts-paris-gregory-christ-ent.notes: Fol. Av is the first of the prefatory leaves (lettered A–C) before the homilies.

cur:monumental-san-samaritan-woman.summary: Seated on a rock beside Jacob's well, the young, haloed Christ in a purple mantle raises his hand in speech towards the Samaritan woman, who draws water with a rope from the well-head under its wooden frame. A disciple in white stands behind him. One of the miracle and teaching scenes high on the north wall of Theodoric's palace church, it distils a long Gospel dialogue about 'living water' into a single quiet encounter.
facts: The thirteen scenes of the north wall show Christ's miracles and teaching; in all of them he appears young and beardless, robed in imperial purple.
The scenes were not arranged in biblical order but are thought to follow the Gospel readings of the Lenten liturgy in Theodoric's palace church.
